review.note: Synoptic revision for Section B. Draws on key topics 1–5.

learn.intro: Section B essays ask you to compare periods and judge change over time. Use this topic to see each of the five specification themes across all five key topics, with the strongest comparative evidence.

sections.title: Theme 1: Congress, the presidency and the Supreme Court

ul: 1865–77: Congress drove change (Reconstruction Acts, 14th and 15th Amendments, Civil Rights Act 1875); Johnson obstructed, Grant enforced; the Court began narrowing protection (Slaughterhouse 1873, Cruikshank 1876).
1883–c1900: the Court enabled Jim Crow (Civil Rights Cases 1883, Plessy 1896, Williams 1898, Cumming 1899); Congress and presidents did nothing.
1933–45: Roosevelt gave relief but avoided civil rights; southern Democrats blocked anti-lynching bills; Executive Order 8802 (1941); the Court began to turn (Gaines 1938, Smith v Allwright 1944).
1954–68: the Court led (Brown 1954); Johnson and Congress delivered the 1964, 1965 and 1968 Acts.
c2000–09: a black President elected; federal law now protected voting and civil rights, though enforcement and outcomes varied.

blocks.p: Judgement prompt: federal institutions were most decisive when all three branches moved together (1865–70, 1964–68) and most damaging when the Court acted alone against black rights (1883–1899).

evidence: Plessy 1896 vs Brown 1954: the Court reversing itself.
Civil Rights Act 1875 struck down 1883 vs Civil Rights Act 1964 upheld.

sections.title: Theme 2: Pressure groups and individuals

ul: 1865–77: black officeholders (Revels, Bruce) and Radical Republicans in Congress.
1883–c1900: Booker T. Washington's accommodationism; Ida B. Wells against lynching; Plessy's test case.
1933–45: NAACP legal campaign and anti-lynching work; Randolph's March on Washington Movement; CORE (1942); Double V.
1954–68: NAACP, SCLC, SNCC, CORE, King, Malcolm X, Black Power.
c2000–09: black politicians and voters; Obama's campaign organisation.

blocks.p: Judgement prompt: pressure groups achieved most when they forced federal action (1941, 1963–65); on their own, as in the 1890s, they could not overcome hostile state governments.

evidence: 1941: threat of a march → Executive Order 8802.

ul: 1865–77: Black Codes, Ku Klux Klan, White League, Redeemer Democrats.
1883–c1900: state legislatures, disfranchisement, lynching at its peak.
1933–45: southern Democrats in Congress (seniority, filibusters); race riots (Detroit 1943).
1954–68: massive resistance, Citizens' Councils, the Klan, northern white backlash.
c2000–09: continuing tensions over policing; hostility after 2008 (birther theory).

blocks.p: Judgement prompt: resistance was most effective when it controlled state governments and Congress (1877–1945); it was weakened when federal power was used against it.

ul: 1865–77: freedom but landlessness; sharecropping and crop liens; Freedmen's Bureau schools, black colleges.
1883–c1900: underfunded segregated schools (Cumming 1899); debt peonage, convict leasing; Tuskegee.
1933–45: New Deal relief and jobs (WPA, PWA) but AAA evictions and NRA wage differentials; war-industry jobs.
1954–68: Brown v Board; rising incomes and college enrolment for some; ghettos persist; Civil Rights Act 1964 bans job discrimination.
c2000–09: a substantial black middle class but wide wealth and poverty gaps.

sections.title: Theme 5: Settlement and housing

ul: 1865–77: freedom of movement; most freedpeople stayed in the rural South.
1883–c1900: a modest drift north and west; most black Americans still southern and rural.
1933–45: Great Migration earlier in the century created northern urban communities; renewed migration to war industries; ghettos, restrictive covenants.
1954–68: urban ghettos; riots (Watts 1965); Fair Housing Act 1968.
c2000–09: more than half of black Americans in the South again; suburbanisation of the middle class.

evidence: 2000: over half of black Americans live in the South.

vocab.def: Linking several periods in one argument.
A moment after which the direction of change altered.
What stayed the same across periods.

misconceptions.right: Rights were won, lost after 1877 and in the 1890s, and only restored after 1954.

mcq.q: In which period did the Supreme Court do most to advance civil rights?
mcq.why: Brown v Board (1954) and backing for desegregation.

mcq.q: What was the main obstacle to civil rights in Congress in 1933–45?
Which case shows 'equal' was not enforced in education before Brown?
mcq.why: A black high school closed while white ones stayed open.

short.q: Which 1954 case reversed Plessy in education?

short.answer: The Fair Housing Act (Civil Rights Act 1968)

chronology.title: Put the Supreme Court decisions in order

matching.title: Match the period to its main resisting force

evidence.q: Give two pieces of evidence that the Supreme Court both hindered and helped civil rights.
evidence.model: Hindered: Civil Rights Cases (1883), Plessy (1896). Helped: Smith v Allwright (1944), Brown (1954).

flashcards.q: When did all three branches of federal government support civil rights together?
When were pressure groups most effective?
flashcards.a: When they forced federal action — 1941 (Executive Order 8802), 1963–65 (Birmingham, Selma).
White southern control of state governments and, through seniority, of key congressional committees.

flashcards.q: What was the main economic continuity from 1865 to 1945?
flashcards.a: Most black southerners remained poor agricultural workers — sharecroppers and tenants — with limited education.
Rural South → northern cities (Great Migration) → many back to a now-urban South; middle-class suburbanisation.

checklist.text: I can compare the role of Congress, the presidency and the Supreme Court across at least two periods.
I can compare the impact of pressure groups and individuals across periods.
I can compare the forces resisting civil rights across periods.
I can explain change and continuity in economic and educational opportunity.
I can explain changing patterns of settlement and housing.
